newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks to mark time as U.S. worries dominate.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks to mark time as U.S. worries dominate.

text.p: A faltering U.S. stock market looks likely to take the wind out of London shares again next week after a string of losses on Wall Street in recent days, London strategists said on Friday.
But any setback in the UK is expected to be modest with dealers confident that sustained weakness will merely draw more money into the equities from cash-rich institutional investors.
U.S. October non-farm payroll numbers loom at the end of the week and worries of what that will bring may prolong the disappointingly patchy performance of recent sessions.
The FTSE 100 has struggled since setting its latest all-time high on Monday of 4,073.2 points, and on Thursday slipped back below the 4,000 mark for the first time in two weeks.

Profit-taking on Wall Street has been largely to blame and four straight losing sessions has pulled the Dow below 6,000 points, doing much to puncture the bouyant mood in London. Dealers, noting a swing in sentiment in London over recent days, suggest further falls are a possibility but say concerns at the recent setback in the market should not be overdone.
"You will have nervous bouts from time to time but there are too many people out there sitting with surplus cash," said the head of equity trading at one leading brokerage.
In another thin week for domestic data, the health of the U.S. economy is once again set to dominate with Friday's U.S. jobs figures topping the agenda in a packed U.S. diary.
Friday also sees the release of U.S. leading indicators, factory goods and both the U.S. and UK purchasing managers indices. U.S income and spending data is out on Thursday.

"There's nervousness on a number of issues. One of them is Wall Street. Another is the domestic economy and whether rates are going to go up or ought to go up. The market has run out of momentum and it is quite easily spooked at the moment," said Richard Jeffrey, strategist at Charterhouse Tilney.
Jeffrey, who puts the possibility of a rate rise after next week's monthly monetary meeting on October 30 at 50/50, believes an early hike in rates would benefit markets long term.
"Shares may have an adverse reaction initially but it would help reassure people that the government's not going to let things get out of hand."
Inflationary pressures may be muted at the moment but if interest rates are left at present levels, the concern is that problems may surface further down the line.
"The next two to three months might be OK, it's after that people will have to worry," said Nomura strategist Allison Southey.
"Whoever wins the next election is probably going to have to raise rates as soon as they get in because they're being held at present levels too long."

Strategist year-end targets for the FTSE 100 range between 4,200 down to Nomura's 3,600 with many bunched around the 4,000 mark. Charterhouse's Jeffrey, one of those on 4,000, says on an earnings basis the market looks fully- though not over-valued and that a five percent overshoot of his target is a possibility.

"But the market would find it very difficiult to hold that level and would be very vulnerable to profit taking. The problem is that a lot of institutions didn't expect it to get up to 4,000 and at that level they don't feel a very strong requirement to put money in."
